extracted.intended_audience: computer science and mathematics students writing technical/academic papers (students in Don's CS writing course)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for composing clear, correct, and reader-aware mathematical and computer-science term papers and expository writing, with emphasis on punctuation, terminology, structure, and use of style tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: which vs. that (restrictive vs non-restrictive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'that' for defining/restrictive clauses and 'which' for non-defining/non-restrictive clauses; if you can substitute 'that' for 'which', do it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Class exercise: write a sentence that uses 'that' correctly where 'which' would be wrong, and one that uses 'which' correctly where 'that' would be incorrect. Strunk & White / Lamport rule: 'If it sounds all right to replace a 'which' by a 'that', then replace it.' Applies to everyday expository prose (not literary prose). Tone is affected by these tiny choices; unnecessary 'which' can make writing sound nervous. Examples: 'All the students that know when to use 'which' and 'that' will pass the quiz.' vs 'The exam, which took place at the beginning of class, was not difficult.'

rubrics_metrics.name: subheadings must be independent
rubrics_metrics.description: The text should make sense if read through omitting the titles of subsections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not refer to the subheading as an integral part of the sentence. Instead of '2. Contour Integration. This technique, invented by Cauchy, is used...', write '2. Contour Integration. The technique of integrating along curves in the complex plane, invented by Cauchy, is used...' Treat subheadings as marginal/meta-level notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: define terms clearly and early
rubrics_metrics.description: Define your graph-theory / mathematical terms clearly at the start, even the most basic ones, because different authors use terms inconsistently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: path vs simple path vs walk — state definitions up front. Ask what background your readers share. If you intend to use a symbol that might not be universally known (e.g., '=' historically), define it at the beginning. Avoid defining symbols/terms you never use.

rubrics_metrics.name: be succinct (less is more)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer shorter, clearer definitions and statements when possible; condense multi-part definitions if parts are unused elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: shorten a long multi-part definition by removing parts (W2 unused) to make the expression less formidable. Don's maxim: 'Less is more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: consistency of terminology (especially with co-authors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be consistent in the names you use for concepts; coordinate terminology across co-authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using different terms for the same concept (e.g., one author uses 'dominators' and another 'parents'). If symbols or names clash, invent another name rather than overloading notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: don't define unused terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid defining concepts or symbols that you never use in the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feynman/New Math example: teaching symbols long before meaningful use is confusing. Only introduce what you'll actually use.

rubrics_metrics.name: use simple rules rather than needlessly complex optimal ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer a simple rule or statement over a more complex, marginally-more-accurate one that burdens the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: omit 'j > 0' when H0 already satisfies the condition; give a simple rule rather than an optimal or convoluted qualification.

rubrics_metrics.name: tense and factual statements about algorithms/problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Use tense appropriately: algorithms (or results about them) are timeless facts ('have' not 'had'), whereas problems may have historical changes in known complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite ambiguous sentences to make logic clearer: e.g., 'Gabow and Tarjan have shown how to improve the algorithms by removing such a multiplicative factor from the worst-case complexities in many cases [Gab83].' Also avoid mixing terms ('multiplicative factor' vs 'multiplicative term').

rubrics_metrics.name: citation formatting and parenthetical references
rubrics_metrics.description: References should ideally be parenthetical so sentences read sensibly without them; be careful of spacing around citation brackets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constructs like 'Tarjan[Gab83]' with no space, or 'In [Smith 80] it was shown...' References should let the sentence be readable without them. Consider citation style implications when republishing in different formats; tools like TeX/BibTeX automate numbering/spacing. Chicago Manual tip: leave references unnumbered to avoid renumbering pain.

rubrics_metrics.name: comma usage guided by speech pauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't overuse commas; a rough guide is to put a comma where a speaker would pause to draw breath.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example correction: 'Our algorithm to recognize and label the graphs when given a directed graph, G, with distinguished vertex s, can be summarized as follows.' — remove commas around 'G' and place one after 'graphs'.

rubrics_metrics.name: hyphenate compound adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Use hyphens to form clear compound adjectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write 'one-vertex path' instead of 'one vertex path'.

rubrics_metrics.name: use correct prepositions and spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer clearer prepositions and ensure spacing in references and parentheticals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: use 'vertex at distance < d' rather than 'vertex of distance < d'. Insert spaces where needed: 'using 4.3 (below) we derive ...' (need space between '4.3' and '(below)').

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid ambiguous words / unfortunate coincidences
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of words that have multiple senses in your context and choose less ambiguous wording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: replace ambiguous 'loop' with 'self-loop'; avoid 'the node x is left' which could mean direction or past tense. Avoid mixing domain words with homonyms (airplanes vs complex planes).

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid using unproved lemmas/theorems prematurely
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not invoke a lemma or theorem that is proved later without clear indication; respect logical partial ordering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using results before they are proved can leave readers suspicious; explicitly indicate dependencies or reorder proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: pluralization and genitive for symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Form plurals and possessives of symbols carefully to avoid ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'the Hj's' (which conflicts when using primes like H' j). Prefer 'each Hj is ...' or invent another name. For possessive, use an apostrophe correctly (e.g., 'Hj's descendants').

rubrics_metrics.name: use ties (non-breaking spaces) to control line breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: Use TeX ties (non-breaking spaces) to keep related words/symbols from being split across lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put ties after 'dominates' in 'v dominates x and x dominates w', and between 'e' and 'is' in '. . . if e is . . .', to prevent line breaks that distort meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: examples should build incrementally
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer a sequence of examples that build upon one another rather than a set of unrelated examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A progressive sequence of illustrations aids understanding more than isolated examples; praised in Haddad and Schäffer's paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: use of style/readability metrics (computer aids)
rubrics_metrics.description: Style programs compute readability grades and other surface statistics based on average words per sentence and syllables per word; these metrics are superficial but useful to prompt revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readability grade = α(words/sentence) + β(syllables/word) + γ, where α,β,γ are regression-derived constants. Programs also report average sentence length, percentage of sentences much shorter/longer than average, sentence-type frequencies, percentages of nouns/adjectives/verbs, and flag passive voice. Aim to minimize grade level moderately — don't overdo it. These tools are shallow but worthwhile to force a re-read from another angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: diction program / flagged words
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction utilities flag a set of 'questionable' words/phrases (e.g., 'gratuitous', 'number of', 'due to') and invite alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat flags as prompts to reconsider word choice; be aware that such tools may not respect field-specific usages (e.g., mathematical 'due to' to credit a theorem). Copy-editors' preferences vary and may conflict with technical usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: be aware of passive voice counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Style tools often count passive constructions (anywhere a passive verb appears) to flag heavy passive usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passive voice may be appropriate in technical writing but be mindful of overuse; e.g., long technical expositions may score high for passivity even if stylistically acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: tone matters: many tiny choices affect readership
rubrics_metrics.description: Small stylistic choices (punctuation, which/that, diction) collectively shape tone and reader engagement; getting many small choices wrong reduces readership and attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mary-Claire: 'tone consists entirely of making these tiny, tiny choices.' Readers who don't have to read will stop if tone is wrong; those who must read will do so with less attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: use exercises and calisthenics to develop style, but choose useful ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing exercises (e.g., verse exercises, rhetorical term practice) can build facility, but avoid exercises that don't transfer to useful writing skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mary-Claire recommends certain prosody and rhetorical-term exercises but warns some exercises (e.g., those that don't help) are not profitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: use editorial judgment when following authority/rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Guides (Fowler, Strunk & White, New Yorker house style) influence practice, but obeying blindly is not always best — apply judgment and be aware of audience and context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical note: Fowler's prescriptions were influential; Strunk & White simplified rules for American audiences. The class notes counsel awareness of obedience vs. informed choice; e.g., some 'wicked whiches' in great authors reflect stylistic choices rather than ignorance.
